title.analysis: Authentic title "Shocking Money Stats of the Average American" uses a list/statistics frame with a "shocking" intensifier and a social-comparison hook. The script delivers a rapid sequence of household finance statistics. It underperformed a cohort that contains the channel's viral threshold titles ("How Everything Changes After You Save $10,000", "Why Everything Changes EVEN MORE After $20,000"). The later "50 Shocking Money Stats Of The Average Person" reused the frame. WEAK against the cohort; association only, no CTR or experiment evidence.

script.stored_text_completeness: All 19157 canonical characters read sequentially in full in 1 bounded ranges; auto-generated untimed text; stored ending is complete ("actually do something about it."); ASR number garbles ("$15,000" vs later "$100,000" debt; income "just over $11,000" with "six figures"; "$1.46 46 million"; "$35100"); the $1,500 non-essentials passage is repeated; fillers ("Um", "Uh"); audio, timed delivery and editing unverified.
script.opening_words: Picture this. You wake up tomorrow morning and suddenly you can see everyone's bank account balance floating above their heads like some twisted video game. The barista making your coffee. Your coworker complaining about being broke. That neighbor with the shiny new car they're always washing. What would you discover? Would you be horrified by how little most people actually have saved? Or would you realize you're doing way worse than you thought? Well, I've got some news for you.
script.ending_words: key is understanding that average doesn't have to be your destiny. With some basic financial discipline and the willingness to make different choices than the majority, you can easily outperform these statistics and build the kind of financial security that most people only dream about. The question isn't whether it's possible to do better than average. It's whether you're ready to stop making excuses and actually do something about it.
script.analysis: Full 19157 canonical characters read. A statistics roundup: bank-balances-over-heads hook, household debt, income and spending, housing (30% rule), transportation and car payments, non-essential spending, emergency savings, retirement magic number vs savings, Social Security, survey attitudes, FICO, card debt, first-time buyers and home prices, student loans, monthly debt service and an invest-instead counterfactual, repeated non-essentials passage, near-retiree medians and a 4% example, income by age, and a close. Verified: Northwestern Mutual 2024 $1.46M / $88,400; CE average income ~$101,805 (2023). Wrong or stale: first-time buyer age (36 vs record 38), $1,200 at 8% for 30 years (~$1.79M, not $2.7M), Social Security average ($1,550 vs ~$2,000), retirement medians (2019 SCF), home price ($350K), spending $6,270 not matching CE 2023. Internal inconsistencies: debt $15,000 vs $100,000; 40% called "nearly half". Several numbers are ASR-garbled. Most simple multiplications reproduce. The stored ending is complete.
beat_map: Hook: everyone's bank balance floating above their heads.
Housing: first-time buyer age, home price, home size.
Near-retirees: medians, 4% and Social Security total.
